# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 7, 2026
**Re:** Taisund Event Rentals, LLC: review of the Stepisk contract documents and the October 19, 2026 assignment notice

---

## 1. Summary

I reviewed the five documents in the matter folder:

- the Exclusive Distribution Agreement dated March 2, 2026 (the **"Agreement"** or **"DA"**);
- the Statement of Work for refurbishment, warehousing and logistics dated March 16, 2026 (**"SOW"**);
- the Service Level Schedule dated March 16, 2026 (**"SLS"**);
- Stepisk's notice letter dated October 19, 2026 (the **"Notice Letter"**); and
- the March 19, 2026 kickoff meeting notes.

I found three material issues. They are listed below in order of how much they matter to Taisund now. I weighed the size of the exposure against how soon Taisund has to act.

| # | Issue | Location | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Stepisk may assign the Agreement freely, including to a competitor. It has given notice that it will assign to Orlenne Event Group LLC effective **December 1, 2026**. | DA §17.2; Notice Letter | **Urgent. Action needed now.** |
| 2 | Taisund's product indemnity covers even claims caused by Stepisk's product defects, and it is **uncapped**. | DA §10.1 and §12.2 (with §12.1, §12.3) | **High. Exposure is structural and ongoing.** |
| 3 | The SOW chooses New York law and New York County courts, and it **overrides** the Delaware choice because of the order of precedence. | SOW §9.1; DA §2.3, §§18.1–18.2 | **Medium. Fix in the same amendment.** |

**Why Issue 1 comes first.** Issue 2 is arguably the largest dollar exposure. Issue 1 comes first because the assignment takes effect in about three weeks, Taisund has no contractual veto, and its leverage drops sharply once the transfer happens. The amendment Taisund seeks on Issue 1 is also the natural place to fix Issues 2 and 3.

The kickoff meeting notes are operational only. They expressly record (¶2.2) that no changes to the contract documents were proposed or agreed. They do not alter any of the analysis below.

---

## 2. Action Items and Decisions for Taisund (Time-Sensitive)

> **ACTION REQUIRED – before December 1, 2026 (Assignment Date):**
> 1. **Decide promptly** whether Taisund objects to the assignment to Orlenne. Our recommendation is that it should. Send a written response to Stepisk's General Counsel under DA §19.1 (hand, courier or certified mail, with a copy by email). The response should do three things:
>    - reserve all rights;
>    - state that Taisund does not consent; and
>    - demand assurances about confidentiality and the exclusivity covenant (see Issue 1).
>
>    Taisund should not sign any acknowledgment, consent or transition document, and should not take steps that could be read as acceptance, until we advise.
> 2. **Instruct operations staff now.** Marisol Quennet, who is copied on the Notice Letter, should be told not to agree anything with Orlenne or Stepisk about the transition. Staff should keep sending Forecasts and Purchase Orders only to Stepisk, as the letter itself directs (Notice Letter §5.1). Taisund should also consider limiting the Customer-specific delivery detail it gives Stepisk to what performance strictly requires.
> 3. **Decide negotiating posture.** Taisund should decide whether to seek a package amendment covering assignment, the indemnity/cap and governing law, and what it will trade for it. One possible concession is the minimum purchase commitment in DA §5.2.
> 4. **Insurance check.** Ask Taisund's broker to confirm whether Taisund's CGL policy covers the contractual liability assumed in DA §10.1, and up to what limit. The contractual minimum is only $1M per occurrence and $2M aggregate (DA §11.2).

---

## 3. Issues

### Issue 1: Stepisk can assign the Agreement to anyone, including a competitor, and is about to do so

**Where:** DA §17.2 (compare §17.1). The Notice Letter dated October 19, 2026, §§1.2, 2.2, 3 and 4.

**What the documents say**
- **Taisund needs consent; Stepisk does not.** Under DA §17.1, Taisund cannot assign without Stepisk's prior written consent. DA §17.2, by contrast, provides that "Supplier may assign this Agreement, in whole or in part, to any person, including by merger, consolidation, reorganization or sale of all or any part of its assets or business, **without the consent of Distributor**, upon written notice to Distributor."
- **No protections for Taisund.** There is no competitor exclusion, no change-of-control protection, and no right for Taisund to terminate on assignment.
- **The assignment terms.** The Notice Letter dated **October 19, 2026** is expressly given under §17.2. It states that Stepisk will assign the Agreement, the SOW and the SLS to **Orlenne Event Group LLC**, effective **December 1, 2026**.
- **Orlenne is a direct competitor.** Orlenne operates an event furniture rental business serving venues, caterers, planners and corporate customers in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware. That is the Territory under DA §3.1.
- **Stepisk keeps manufacturing.** Stepisk will continue to make the Products and will supply them to Orlenne for fulfillment (Notice Letter §3.3).
- **Taisund's data goes to Orlenne.** Stepisk will hand Orlenne the following (Notice Letter §4.1):
  - Taisund's pricing and SOW fees;
  - Forecasts and open Purchase Orders;
  - buffer plans and inventory reports;
  - **Customer delivery schedules and locations**; and
  - service level records.

**Why it matters to Taisund**
- **Commercial harm.** Taisund's sole supplier, and its whole logistics chain (refurbishment, buffer stock, delivery runs, damaged-unit replacement), would be controlled by its direct competitor in its own exclusive Territory. Orlenne would see Taisund's costs, demand, and Customer identities and event locations. Orlenne would also have an incentive to under-perform, for example on the 48-hour replacement time in SLS §2.2 or the expedited deliveries in SLS §3.3. The service credits, capped at 20% of monthly services fees (SLS §8.2), are a weak deterrent.
- **No contractual veto.** Taisund cannot block the assignment on the face of §17.2. It must **not** proceed on the premise that Stepisk needs its consent.
- **The assignment has not yet occurred, and nothing in the folder shows Taisund has consented.** So there is still a window to act.

**Points of leverage despite §17.2**
- **Exclusivity covenant (DA §3.2).** Stepisk may not, "directly or through any Affiliate or third party," sell or rent Products in the Territory other than through Taisund, or appoint another rental operator there. If Orlenne becomes "Supplier," it would take on that covenant. Its own rental business would breach §3.2 to the extent it rents Products, and possibly comparable Stepisk lines. Stepisk's supply of Products to a competing Territory rental operator also needs scrutiny under §3.2.
- **Confidentiality (DA §14.2).** Confidential Information may be used *only* to perform the Agreement. Taisund should demand written undertakings from Orlenne before any data transfer. These should include ethical walls between Orlenne's logistics function and its rental sales function. The data covered includes Customer delivery schedules and locations, which DA §14.1 expressly makes confidential.
- **Most favored pricing (DA §6.2) and the warranty, remedy and insurance obligations (DA §§8, 11.1).** We should confirm whether Stepisk intends to remain liable for these after the assignment. The letter says Orlenne assumes obligations accruing only *from and after* the Assignment Date (§3.2). Absent a novation, Stepisk as assignor should generally remain liable for its obligations, including the 36-month product warranty. Taisund should insist on that expressly.
- **Termination routes.** Taisund has the existing rights in DA §15.1 (material breach, 30-day cure) and §15.3 (repeated service failures). If Orlenne breaches §3.2 or §14, these provide a path out.

**Recommended fix**
1. **Immediate written objection and reservation of rights.** This is the action item above. The letter should demand:
   - confirmation that Stepisk remains jointly liable;
   - Orlenne's written assumption of §§3.2, 6.2 and 14;
   - information-barrier undertakings; and
   - suspension of the data transfer under Notice Letter §4.1 pending agreement.
2. **Negotiate an amendment to §17.2** that:
   - requires Taisund's prior written consent to any assignment or change of control of Stepisk (mutual with §17.1);
   - flatly prohibits assignment to any person who competes with Taisund in the Territory, or its affiliates; and
   - gives Taisund a right to terminate without penalty, with an extended sell-off and transition period, on any assignment or change of control it has not approved.
3. **Contingency planning.** If Stepisk will not move, Taisund should evaluate:
   - substitute supply sources;
   - its §15 termination rights; and
   - whether to seek injunctive relief to protect Confidential Information. DA §18.4 allows this without first going through executive escalation.

**Facts to confirm with the client**
- Whether Taisund has responded to the Notice Letter or said anything, orally or in writing, that could be construed as acceptance.
- Whether Orlenne currently rents Stepisk Products, or competing lines, in the Territory.
- Whether Orlenne is an Affiliate of Stepisk, and what the "broader commercial arrangement" in Notice Letter §2.2 involves.
- What Confidential Information Stepisk has already shared with Orlenne.
- How long it would take Taisund to replace Stepisk as a supplier.

---

### Issue 2: Taisund's product indemnity reaches defect-caused claims and is uncapped

**Where:** DA §10.1 and §12.2, read with §12.1, §12.3 and §10.2.

**What the documents say**
- **Taisund's indemnity is very broad.** DA §10.1 requires Taisund to defend and indemnify Stepisk and its Affiliates against all claims arising out of "the distribution, rental, setup or use of the Products by Distributor, any Customer or any other person, **regardless of whether caused by a defect in the Products**."
- **Stepisk's indemnity is narrow.** DA §10.2 covers only third-party IP infringement claims.
- **The cap.** DA §12.1 caps each party's liability at **the amounts paid or payable under the Agreement in the 12 months before the claim**.
- **The carve-out.** DA §12.2 provides that the cap "shall not apply to a party's obligations under Section 10."
- **Consequential damages.** DA §12.3 also removes §10 obligations from the consequential-damages exclusion.

**Why it matters to Taisund**
- **The carve-out only looks mutual.** In practice it works against Taisund. Consider a guest injured when a defectively manufactured chiavari chair or folding table collapses. That is a scenario squarely within Stepisk's 36-month defect warranty in DA §8.1(b) and its BIFMA compliance warranty in DA §8.2. Taisund would still have to defend and pay Stepisk's liability, with **no cap** and including consequential losses.
- **Stepisk's carved-out exposure is limited** to narrow IP claims.
- **The indemnity extends to Affiliates.** That reach would expand if the Agreement is assigned to Orlenne, and it covers claims by "any other person."
- **Insurance does not close the gap.** Taisund's required CGL limits are only $1M per occurrence (DA §11.2). Stepisk carries products and completed operations coverage (DA §11.1). But Taisund is not named as an additional insured, and §10.1 effectively shifts Stepisk's products risk onto Taisund in any event.
- **The cap could also be very large.** It is measured on amounts "paid or payable," and the minimum purchase commitment alone is $1.2M per year (DA §5.2). That cap applies to Taisund's other liabilities, while Taisund's indemnity has no ceiling at all.

**Recommended fix**
1. **Narrow §10.1** to claims caused by Taisund's own negligence, misuse, or failure to follow Stepisk's instructions (§9.2). Expressly exclude claims caused by design, manufacturing or material defects, by breach of §8, or by Stepisk's refurbishment work or negligence under SOW §3.
2. **Add a reciprocal Stepisk indemnity** for product liability, personal injury and property damage claims arising from Product defects, non-compliance with §8.2, or defective refurbishment.
3. **Narrow the §12.2 and §12.3 carve-outs.** Either:
   - make only third-party indemnities for matters within the indemnitor's control uncapped; or
   - subject Taisund's §10.1 indemnity to a defined cap, such as a multiple of the §12.1 amount or Taisund's available insurance.
4. **Require Stepisk to name Taisund as an additional insured** on its products and completed operations policy under DA §11.1, and to waive subrogation.

**Facts to confirm with the client**
- Any incidents, injuries or claims to date involving the Products.
- Taisund's actual insurance program, including any contractual liability endorsement and umbrella coverage.
- Annual spend under the Agreement and SOW, so we can size the cap.

---

### Issue 3: The SOW's New York law and forum clause overrides the Agreement's Delaware clause

**Where:** SOW §9.1, read with DA §2.3 and DA §§18.1–18.2.

**What the documents say**
- **The Agreement chooses Delaware.** DA §18.1 chooses Delaware law. DA §18.2 gives exclusive jurisdiction to the state or federal courts in Wilmington, Delaware.
- **The SOW chooses New York.** SOW §9.1 provides that the SOW, and any dispute "arising out of or relating to this SOW or the Services," is governed by the **laws of the State of New York**. It gives exclusive jurisdiction to the state or federal courts in **New York County**.
- **The order of precedence favors the SOW.** Under DA §2.3, conflicts among the Contract Documents are resolved in this order: **Statement of Work first, then Service Level Schedule, then Distribution Agreement.** The SOW therefore prevails. For disputes within its scope (refurbishment, warehousing and delivery of inventory), New York law and the New York County forum control. Delaware law and the Wilmington forum govern the rest of the relationship.

**Why it matters to Taisund**
- **Disputes could be split.** The likeliest real-world dispute is damaged, late or lost inventory. Such a dispute would involve all of the following at once:
  - the SOW (delivery, bailment and risk in storage under §4.4, refurbishment warranty under §3.5);
  - the SLS (replacement time, service credits); and
  - the Agreement's warranties, indemnity, cap and termination rights.

  Two *exclusive* forum clauses under two bodies of law invite threshold fights over where a claim belongs. They also raise the risk of parallel litigation, inconsistent results and added cost.
- **The SLS adds a further wrinkle.** SLS §7.3 routes unresolved disputes to DA §18.3 escalation, which assumes the Agreement's dispute framework.
- **The assignment adds a third.** Any service-related claim against Orlenne after December 1 could be pushed to New York, which is neutral for neither party. Both Stepisk and Orlenne are Delaware entities, and Taisund is in Philadelphia.

**Recommended fix**
- Delete SOW §9.1, or replace it with a cross-reference to DA §18.
- Alternatively, amend DA §2.3 to provide that **Section 18 of the Agreement controls notwithstanding the order of precedence** and any contrary provision in the SOW or SLS.
- Taisund should also consider whether it would rather have the Agreement's precedence order run the other way generally. Under the current order, any SOW or SLS term can override the Agreement's protections, which is an ongoing drafting risk.

**Facts to confirm with the client**
- Whether the SOW's New York clause was deliberately negotiated.
- Whether any service dispute is pending or anticipated. Several possible claims involve Damage Reports and replacement timing, and their forum should be settled before they ripen.
- Taisund's preferred forum. It may prefer Pennsylvania to Delaware.

---

## 4. Other Observations (Lower Priority)

- **Executed copies.** The folder versions show signature blocks with names and dates but blank signature lines. We should obtain the fully executed copies of all three Contract Documents. The SOW and SLS take effect as part of the Agreement only "upon signature by both parties" (DA §2.2).
- **Renewal.** The Initial Term runs three years from March 2, 2026, with automatic one-year renewals unless either party gives 180 days' notice (DA §4.2). Nothing is due now. The calendar date for non-renewal notice should be diarized, particularly if the Orlenne assignment proceeds.

---

## 5. Recommended Next Steps

1. **This week:** send Taisund's written objection and reservation of rights to Stepisk under DA §19.1. Brief the client on the points in Section 2.
2. **Before December 1, 2026:** propose a single amendment covering:
   - §17.2 (consent, competitor bar, termination right);
   - §§10.1, 10.2, 12.2 and 12.3 (indemnity scope and cap);
   - §11.1 (additional insured); and
   - SOW §9.1 or DA §2.3 (governing law and forum).
3. **In parallel:** collect the facts flagged above from Taisund, and begin contingency planning on alternative supply and on its §15 and §18.4 remedies.

Please let me know if you would like a draft of the objection letter or the amendment.

# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 7, 2026
**Re:** Taisund Event Rentals, LLC / Stepisk Furnishings Manufacturing, Inc.: review of contract documents and the October 19, 2026 assignment notice

---

## 1. Summary

I reviewed the five documents in the matter folder:

- the Exclusive Distribution Agreement dated March 2, 2026 (the **Agreement**);
- the Statement of Work for refurbishment, warehousing and logistics dated March 16, 2026 (the **SOW**);
- the Service Level Schedule dated March 16, 2026 (the **SLS**);
- Stepisk's notice letter dated October 19, 2026 (the **Notice Letter**); and
- the March 19, 2026 kickoff meeting notes.

I identified two substantive issues. I list them below in order of importance to Taisund.

1. **Stepisk can assign the Agreement freely, and it has given notice that it will assign it to Orlenne Event Group LLC, a direct competitor in the Territory.** The assignment takes effect on **December 1, 2026**, which is about three weeks from today. This is the most urgent and most commercially significant issue.
2. **The SOW's New York governing law and forum clause overrides the Agreement's Delaware clause for SOW-scope disputes.** This is because of the order of precedence in Agreement Section 2.3. The result is that the relationship is split between two laws and two exclusive forums.

The kickoff meeting notes are operational only. They expressly record that no changes to the contract documents were proposed or agreed (Notes §2.2), so they do not affect either issue. Nothing in the folder shows that Taisund has consented to the Orlenne assignment or acknowledged it.

---

## 2. Action Required / Decisions Needed Soon

> **URGENT. Assignment Date is December 1, 2026.**
>
> 1. **Decision needed (this week):** Does Taisund object to the Orlenne assignment? Does it want to (a) seek to block or restructure it, (b) negotiate protective amendments as the price of cooperation, or (c) prepare to exit the relationship?
> 2. **Action required (immediately):** Send a written reservation-of-rights and objection letter to Stepisk's General Counsel under Agreement Section 19.1, with a copy to Orlenne. The letter should state that Taisund does not consent, and it should demand that no Taisund Confidential Information be transferred to Orlenne pending discussion (see Issue 1).
> 3. **Action required:** Instruct Taisund's operations staff, including Marisol Quennet, not to sign, countersign or "acknowledge" any transition documents, new payment instructions or Orlenne paperwork without our review. A course of dealing could later be characterized as acceptance.
> 4. **Action required:** Consider initiating executive escalation under Agreement Section 18.3. The senior executives' meeting must take place within 15 business days of notice, so a notice sent now would bring that meeting before December 1.
> 5. **Decision needed (medium term):** Should Taisund seek to fix the SOW governing law conflict (Issue 2) as part of any amendment negotiated in connection with the assignment?

---

## 3. Issues

### Issue 1: Unrestricted assignment by Stepisk, and pending assignment to a competitor (Orlenne)

**Where it appears**

- Agreement **Section 17.2** (Assignment by Supplier), read against Section 17.1.
- **Notice Letter dated October 19, 2026**, §§1.2, 2.2, 3.1–3.3 and 4.1.

**What the documents say**

- Section 17.1 bars *Taisund* from assigning without Stepisk's prior written consent. It also voids any non-compliant assignment.
- Section 17.2 is asymmetrical. It provides that "Supplier may assign this Agreement, in whole or in part, to any person, including by merger, consolidation, reorganization or sale of all or any part of its assets or business, **without the consent of Distributor**, upon written notice to Distributor."
- The Agreement contains none of the following:
  - a carve-out barring assignment to competitors;
  - any requirement that the assignee be creditworthy or capable of performing;
  - a change-of-control provision; or
  - a right for Taisund to terminate following an assignment.
- The Notice Letter, given expressly under Sections 17.2 and 19.1, states that:
  - Stepisk *will* assign the Agreement, the SOW and the SLS to **Orlenne Event Group LLC**, effective **December 1, 2026** (Letter §3.1);
  - Orlenne "operates an event furniture rental business" serving venues, caterers, planners and corporate customers in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware (Letter §2.2). That is the same customer base as Taisund's, in the same Territory (Agreement §3.1);
  - Orlenne will receive Taisund's pricing, Forecasts, open Purchase Orders, buffer plans, inventory reports, Depot schedules, and **Customer delivery schedules and locations** (Letter §4.1);
  - Stepisk will continue to manufacture the Products but will supply them to Orlenne "for fulfillment," so Orlenne steps in between Taisund and the manufacturer (Letter §3.3); and
  - Orlenne assumes only obligations "accruing from and after the Assignment Date" (Letter §3.2).

**Why it matters for Taisund**

- **A competitor becomes Taisund's exclusive supplier and logistics provider.** Orlenne would control the following for Taisund's entire inventory flow:
  - acceptance or rejection of Purchase Orders (§5.4);
  - refurbishment turnaround (SLS §4.2);
  - damaged-unit replacement within 48 hours (SLS §2.2);
  - expedited deliveries; and
  - the buffer inventory held at the Bridgeport warehouse (SOW §4).

  Orlenne would have an obvious incentive to deprioritize Taisund's orders during peak season or to underperform in ways that are hard to prove. Service credits are capped at 20% of Monthly Services Fees (SLS §8.2) and would be little deterrent.
- **Competitively sensitive information passes to a rival.** Section 14 confidentiality would nominally bind Orlenne as successor (Letter §4.2). In practice, Orlenne would hold Taisund's Customer identities, delivery locations, event schedules, forecasts and pricing. Once that information is in a competitor's hands, misuse is difficult to detect and police. Injunctive relief under §18.4 is available, but only after the fact.
- **The commercial terms are exposed.** As "Supplier," Orlenne would hold the price-adjustment right in §6.1 and the fee-adjustment right in SOW §6.3. It would also hold the non-renewal right in §4.2 on 180 days' notice. Notice for the first renewal would fall in 2028, but the leverage exists throughout.
- **Taisund has no contractual exit.** Section 15 allows termination only for uncured material breach, insolvency, or repeated service failures (§15.3). A lawful assignment under §17.2 does not trigger any of these. If Orlenne's performance degrades, Taisund would first have to build a record of SLS failures (three or more months in a rolling 12-month period) before it could leave.
- **Allocation of liability is unclear.** Orlenne assumes only post-Assignment Date obligations. It is not clear whether Stepisk remains liable for pre-assignment obligations or as guarantor of Orlenne's performance. The Agreement does not say that Stepisk is released, and Taisund should not accept a release. Product warranty claims (§8.1, 36 months) relate to goods Stepisk manufactured, and Taisund should insist that Stepisk remain directly responsible for them.
- **"In whole or in part."** Section 17.2 would also permit Stepisk to split the relationship, for example by assigning logistics to Orlenne while keeping supply. That would fragment accountability further.

**Possible arguments and leverage (to be developed)**

- **Section 3.2 exclusivity.** Section 3.2 bars Supplier, "directly or through any Affiliate or third party," from supplying Products to any person for use, resale or rental in the Territory other than through Taisund. If Orlenne would use any Products from Stepisk in its own Territory rental fleet, that would breach §3.2. Stepisk supplying Orlenne "for fulfillment" also risks a breach if the arrangement is not strictly limited to Taisund's orders. We should demand written assurances on this point.
- **Section 14.2 use restriction.** Stepisk may disclose Confidential Information only to persons who "need to know" in order to perform under the Agreement. A pre-Assignment Date transfer of Customer data to Orlenne, before Orlenne has any role, is arguably a breach of Section 14. Breach of Section 14 is excluded from the §12.1 liability cap (§12.2) and from the consequential damages exclusion (§12.3), and it supports injunctive relief under §18.4 without prior escalation.
- **UCC delegation and assurances (Delaware, 6 Del. C. § 2-210).** The Agreement is largely a contract for the sale of goods. Section 2-210 generally permits delegation where the parties have agreed to it, and §17.2 is such an agreement, so this will not block the assignment by itself. However, §2-210 provides that an assignment of "the contract" also delegates performance, and that the other party may treat the assignment as creating reasonable grounds for insecurity and demand assurances from the assignee. We should confirm how this applies to the SOW services component. The SOW is governed by New York law (see Issue 2), so a New York analysis may also be needed.
- **Implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing.** Delaware courts apply this covenant narrowly and will not use it to override express terms such as §17.2. It may still be relevant if the assignment is structured to undermine Taisund's exclusivity.
- **Practical leverage.** Taisund's $1.2 million annual minimum purchase commitment (§5.2) and its role as exclusive Territory distributor are valuable to Stepisk and to the broader "commercial arrangement" with Orlenne (Letter §2.2). Stepisk may prefer a negotiated solution to a dispute.

**Recommended fix**

1. **Immediate:** Send a written objection and reservation of rights to Stepisk before December 1, 2026. The letter should:
   - state that Taisund does not consent;
   - demand that Stepisk not transfer Taisund's Confidential Information to Orlenne;
   - request written assurances on Section 3.2 compliance and on Stepisk's continuing liability; and
   - invoke Section 18.3 escalation.
2. **Negotiated amendment to Section 17.2**, to be sought either as a condition of Taisund's cooperation or in exchange for Taisund's consent to a modified transaction. The amendment should:
   - require Taisund's prior written consent to any assignment or delegation, not to be unreasonably withheld, *except* that Taisund may withhold consent in its sole discretion for any assignment to a competitor of Taisund in the Territory or its Affiliate;
   - treat a change of control of Stepisk in favor of a competitor as an assignment;
   - give Taisund a right to terminate on notice, without penalty and with the §16.3 sell-off rights, if an assignment or change of control occurs without its consent;
   - provide that Stepisk is not released and remains jointly and severally liable with any assignee, with Stepisk remaining directly responsible for product warranty (§8) obligations on Products it manufactures; and
   - impose an information firewall so that Taisund's Customer data, Forecasts and pricing may not be accessed by any assignee's competing rental business.
3. **Fallback if Stepisk insists on proceeding:** Prepare an exit plan. This would include alternative sourcing, reliance on §20.2 substitute-product rights only if force majeure applies, building an SLS performance record for §15.3 purposes, and preserving §16.3 sell-off rights.

**Facts to confirm with the client**

- Has anyone at Taisund responded to the Notice Letter, signed anything from Stepisk or Orlenne, or otherwise indicated acceptance? Has Marisol Quennet, who was copied on the letter, had any conversations with either party?
- What exactly is Orlenne's business? Does it rent or sell chiavari chairs, banquet and cocktail tables, or lounge seating in the Territory? Does it use or plan to use Stepisk Products?
- Has Stepisk already shared any Taisund data with Orlenne?
- What is the "broader commercial arrangement" (Letter §2.2)? Is it an asset sale, a joint venture, or an equity stake? Is Orlenne, or will it become, an Affiliate of Stepisk?
- How dependent is Taisund on Stepisk's Bridgeport warehouse and its buffer inventory? What alternative sources of supply exist?

---

### Issue 2: SOW Section 9.1 selects New York law and New York County courts and overrides the Agreement's Delaware clause

**Where it appears**

- SOW **Section 9.1** (Governing Law and Forum).
- Read together with Agreement **Section 2.3** (Order of Precedence) and **Sections 18.1–18.2** (Governing Law; Forum).

**What the documents say**

- Agreement §18.1 provides that the Agreement is governed by **Delaware** law. Agreement §18.2 submits disputes to the exclusive jurisdiction of the state or federal courts **in Wilmington, Delaware**.
- SOW §9.1 provides that the SOW, "and any claim, controversy or dispute arising out of or relating to this SOW or the Services," is governed by "the laws of the State of New York." It submits such disputes to the **exclusive** jurisdiction of the state or federal courts located in **New York County, New York**.
- Agreement §2.3 sets the **order of precedence**: the **Statement of Work first, then the Service Level Schedule, then the Distribution Agreement**. The Statement of Work therefore prevails over the Agreement in any conflict.
- The SOW and the SLS are each incorporated into the Agreement (§2.2; SOW §10.1; SLS §11.1).

The order-of-precedence clause does not cure the conflict; it makes the conflict worse. Because the SOW ranks first, the New York clause controls for disputes within the SOW's scope. Those are disputes concerning refurbishment, warehousing and delivery of inventory. Delaware law and the Wilmington forum continue to govern the rest of the relationship. It is not correct to say that Delaware law governs SOW disputes on the basis that the Agreement prevails. Under §2.3, it does not.

**Why it matters for Taisund**

- **The most likely disputes fall on the dividing line.** The disputes most likely to arise between Taisund and Stepisk (or Orlenne) concern damaged, late or missing inventory. A single such dispute could involve all of the following at once:
  - SOW delivery and refurbishment obligations (SOW §§3, 5);
  - SLS replacement times and service credits (SLS §§2.2, 8);
  - Agreement delivery, inspection and rejection, and warranty provisions (§§7.3, 8);
  - the Agreement's limitation of liability (§12.1 cap of the amounts paid or payable under the Agreement in the 12 months before the claim); and
  - the termination right for repeated service failures (§15.3).
- **Parallel litigation risk.** One dispute could be split between two *exclusive* forums applying two bodies of law. That creates a risk of parallel proceedings, satellite litigation over which clause governs which claim, increased cost and delay, and inconsistent results.
- **The SLS falls in a gap.** The SLS contains no governing law clause, and it covers both Agreement supply and SOW Services (SLS preamble). It is unclear whether SLS disputes go to New York or to Delaware. The SLS's own dispute route, through Agreement §18.3 (SLS §7.3), adds further ambiguity.
- **Practical inconvenience.** Taisund is based in Philadelphia, and its Depots and the Supplier Warehouse are in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware. Wilmington is close to all of them. Litigating in Manhattan is more costly, and it has no connection to the performance of the SOW.
- **Relevance to Issue 1.** If Taisund ends up in a dispute with Orlenne over transition-period logistics failures, the forum question will arise immediately. The SOW and SLS are expressly included in the proposed assignment (Letter §1.2).
- **Uncertain treatment of the forum clause.** A court in either state may enforce its own exclusive-forum clause and refuse to defer to the other. The result is hard to predict, which is itself a cost.

**Recommended fix**

Seek a short written amendment signed by both parties, as required by Agreement §20.3 and SOW §10.4. The amendment should do one of the following:

- **Option A (preferred):** Delete SOW §9.1 and replace it with a statement that the SOW is governed by Agreement §§18.1–18.4.
- **Option B:** Amend Agreement §2.3 to provide that, notwithstanding the order of precedence, Section 18 of the Agreement governs all Contract Documents and all disputes arising out of or relating to them.

In either case, the amendment should also confirm that the SLS is governed by Agreement Section 18.

The SOW clause benefits neither party in an obvious way, so this should be a relatively easy point to win. It can be bundled with the Issue 1 amendments. If Stepisk resists, Taisund should at minimum ensure that any assignment-related documentation does not repeat or extend the New York clause.

**Facts to confirm with the client**

- Was the New York clause negotiated or discussed, or was it a drafting carry-over from a Stepisk form? Does Stepisk or Orlenne have any New York connection?
- Are there any existing or anticipated claims, such as SLS failures, refurbishment disputes or warehouse inventory discrepancies, that would be affected now?
